title: Boxing match ads, parade jobs and Charlie Cure
summary: Bands advertised fights from trucks, played parades, and a piano player Charlie Cure marched on trumpet.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: You ever go to any boxing matches? Hear bands at boxing matches?

I played for a few, Dick. We used to get on them trucks and go advertise, you know? For the fight. Then you'd go, the band didn't play much at the match. You played more in the truck than you did at the match, you know? As an advertisement.
How long would they have between rounds?
Well, it was a regular boxing like you got now.
Yeah, but I mean, how many courses could you play between the rounds?

Well, they'd just play a, you'd open the fight up when they'd introduce a, just before they introduce a fight, the preliminaries, and the main goal. You'd just play about, maybe about five tunes, four tunes, and then during the whole fight. What you was paid for more than playing there was playing on a truck that you'd play at every corner. You'd see they'd rush you to a corner and stop and play. You might get through a half a course and they'd pull up. You'd go to two corners off and they'd stop again. I didn't like that, man. I didn't like parade jobs either.
Man, dear me, I'd like them parade jobs. You did play a few, though. Oh yeah, you had to, man.

You had to those days. They didn't have that many musicians they could draw from, you know? You know what we used to even do? Get a guy like Charlie Cure, the piano player, and they needed two trumpets and a parade. And you go, all right, Charlie's a trumpet man today. Give him a trumpet, let him march with the trumpets, you know? You know him, Charlie Cure?
A little bit. I used to see him at the St. Charles.
Yeah, I used to play with him, too.
I can't remember what band I played with him with, but I remember playing with Charlie.
